title: Genie Envisioner: unified world foundation for robot grasping
one_liner: A robot learns to grasp and manipulate objects by first watching videos to build intuition, then mapping that intuition into hand motions.
lead: Teaching a robot to grasp a fork, stack blocks, or fold cloth requires learning two things at once: how to understand what it sees, and how to move its hand. Genie Envisioner does both inside a single system that watches real robot videos and learns visual patterns, then converts those patterns into precise finger and arm commands.

problem.h2: Learning vision and motion together is hard
paras: A robot learning to manipulate objects faces two separate challenges: understanding images from its cameras, and translating that understanding into hand motions. The naive approach trains a vision model first (learning what objects look like), then trains a separate control model (learning which movements succeed). But this requires the robot to translate between two different languages: visual patterns from images, and joint angles in the hand. That translation step is error-prone.

Real robot videos contain natural temporal structure—when a hand grasps a cup, the sequence of camera frames shows the hand approaching, touching, gripping, and lifting in a coherent flow. This structure exists in the videos but is wasted if you split vision and control into separate pipelines. The robot ends up re-learning the same temporal dynamics twice.

callout.html: Learn both vision and motion in a single video model, so they share the same internal language and the model sees the full temporal story.

panels.title: 1. The robot watches
panels.caption: Real video: hand approaches, grasps, lifts. One continuous sequence.

panels.title: 2. Naive split pipeline
panels.caption: Two models: one guesses images, one guesses motion. Each relearns the sequence.

panels.title: 3. Unified video model
panels.caption: One model watches and learns: cameras, hand shape, object position, all at once.

panels.title: 4. Extract control from video model
panels.viz_args: Action decoder: video tokens -> finger angles
panels.caption: Lightweight decoder converts video understanding directly into finger commands.

panels.title: 5. Robot generalizes to new embodiments
panels.caption: Same video model works across different robot arms without retraining.

steps.text: Feed video clips to a diffusion transformer (a model trained by adding noise to frames, then learning to remove it). This forces the model to capture spatial patterns (where hands and objects are), temporal patterns (how they move together), and semantic patterns (what the instruction asks for).

The robot has multiple cameras (left, right, front). Instead of treating each camera independently, the model looks at all three at once and compares their views. This lets it build a coherent sense of where objects are in 3D space, because it sees the same hand and cup from different angles and can triangulate their true positions.

Convert the text instruction (e.g., 'grasp the red ball') into a numeric code (the same way any language model encodes words). Then feed this code alongside the video frame codes. The model learns to line up the instruction code with the corresponding video frames—so 'grasp the red ball' connects to frames where the hand actually grasps a red object. This forces the model to learn what each instruction looks like in video form.

steps.b: Step 4: Adapt the video model to a new robot
steps.text: For a different embodiment (e.g., a robot with different arm length), freeze the video backbone and retrain only the action decoder on demonstrations from that new robot. The core visual understanding transfers without relearning from scratch.

steps.b: Step 5: Generate action at test time
steps.text: At test time, one denoising pass through the video model outputs latent frame codes (compressed representations of video frames). The action decoder takes these codes and outputs the sequence of finger joint angles needed to execute the task.

object.h2: What moves: the latent video representation
paras: The paper changes the internal language the robot uses to think about its task. Instead of separate image features and motion primitives, everything is encoded into a single compressed video space—8-frame latent codes learned by a pretrained video encoder. This space naturally captures both 'what the hand is doing' and 'what it will do next,' because it was trained on real video sequences where those always occur together.

hidden.name: cross-embodiment alignment gap
paras: The paper measures a hidden quantity: how much does the visual understanding of a task depend on one specific robot's shape? If you watch a video of Robot A grasping a cup, can Robot B (with different arm length, gripper width, wrist flexibility) execute the same visual plan? The paper's key insight is that diffusion models naturally learn representations that do not depend on one robot's body—they capture the task logic (approach the object, close fingers around it) without baking in one robot's specific arm dimensions, gripper design, or joint types.

The paper estimates this by training the video model on Robot A's 1 million episodes, then adapting to Robot B with only a small labeled dataset of Robot B's trajectories. If the latent video representation is truly embodiment-agnostic, Robot B's action decoder should learn quickly. In ablations, this approach reaches 89% success on end-to-end tasks with cross-embodiment transfer, compared to 30% for models trained only on single embodiments.

heat.caption: Darker means more critical for cross-embodiment transfer. Lightest cells are robot-specific; darkest are universal.

reads.html: A robot learns a reusable visual grammar by watching videos. That grammar doesn't care about joint angles—it cares about hand position, fingers, and target. A different robot can follow the same visual plan by translating those abstract goals into its own body's movement commands.

The video diffusion latent space captures spatiotemporal semantics independent of embodiment kinematics. Task-specific adaptation via frozen visual backbone + fresh action decoder achieves 76–89% success on held-out embodiments, demonstrating embodiment-invariant policy transfer.

mechanism.h2: Why unified video learning enables embodiment transfer
paras: Here is the causal chain. When a robot learns vision and control separately, each model overfits to one robot's body. The vision model sees images of Robot A's gripper and learns 'gripper open' as a pixel pattern. The control model learns 'to grasp, send 150 mA current to motor 3.' When you change to Robot B, both patterns are wrong: Robot B's gripper looks different and has different motors. You have to retrain both from scratch.

A diffusion model trained on video sequences sidesteps this by learning a temporal abstraction layer. Instead of pixel patterns or motor commands, it learns 'the hand moves from position A to position B, with fingers transitioning from spread to closed.' This description works for any robot, because it describes the task goal, not the robot's anatomy. When you freeze the video model and train only a lightweight action decoder on Robot B's data, the decoder merely has to learn Robot B's personal translation guide: 'when the video says hand moves left, send this pattern to Robot B's left motors.' That is a much smaller learning problem, so it succeeds with little data.

The key mechanism is task embodiment-invariance captured in the latent space. A diffusion model's latent codes are optimized for predicting future video frames—a prediction problem that rewards capturing what changes (hand position, object state) and ignoring what doesn't (which specific robot does it). So the representation naturally emphasizes universal task structure.

stages.s: Video clip: robot arm, gripper, object
Compress each camera view into numeric codes using a pretrained encoder
Add instruction text by comparing it to each video frame code
Diffusion model refines video frame codes across multiple denoising steps
Action decoder: tokens -> joint angles for any robot

math.words: During pretraining, the diffusion model learns by predicting clean video frames from noisy ones. During action training, the same latent tokens are fed to an action decoder, which predicts the correct motor commands. The total loss is video reconstruction plus action accuracy, weighted by a balance factor.
math.equation: L_total = L_video(x_clean, x_noisy_t) + lambda * L_action(a_pred, a_true)
symbols: how wrong the predicted frame is compared to the real frame
the video frame with noise added at step t
how wrong the predicted joint angles are compared to ground truth
the actual motor command the robot used
importance weight: higher = care more about action accuracy

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose one video frame has mean squared prediction error of 0.04 (L_video = 0.04).
The action decoder predicts joint angle 75 degrees when true angle is 90 degrees, error squared = 225 = very large error. Summed over all joints, L_action = 2.5.
With lambda = 0.1 (video pretraining dominates early): L_total = 0.04 + 0.1 * 2.5 = 0.29.
With lambda = 1.0 (equal weight later): L_total = 0.04 + 1.0 * 2.5 = 2.54 (action error dominates).
By increasing lambda during training, the model gradually shifts focus from frame prediction to precise control.

math.note: Both the video loss and action loss operate on the same latent codes. When the video model learns clearer frame predictions, the latent codes become more informative (they capture more detail about hand position, object location, gripper angle). The action decoder then sees clearer signals in these codes, so it can learn more accurately which hand position corresponds to which motor command. They reinforce each other.

bars.h2: Success rates: pretraining and adaptation impact

charts.title: Without pretraining (train action from scratch on Robot B alone)
charts.note: The action decoder must learn visual understanding and motor control simultaneously, so it overfits to Robot B's embodiment and fails to generalize.

charts.title: With video pretraining (Genie Envisioner approach)
charts.note: The video model already understands task logic from 1 million diverse episodes. Robot B's action decoder only learns embodiment mapping, a much smaller problem. Generalization is strong because the latent video space captures task invariants.

items.html: If the diffusion model memorizes specific video sequences instead of learning reusable patterns, the latent codes become tied to one robot and one task. Transfer fails because the codes don't generalize. The paper prevents this by pretraining on 1 million diverse episodes with variable frame sampling rates (3–30 Hz), forcing the model to find patterns that work across many different situations and embodiments.

If the text instructions in the dataset are vague or inconsistent, the model cannot reliably connect instructions to video frames. It learns 'grasp' to mean different things on different days, so the action decoder sees conflicting signals about when to grasp. Quality instruction annotation is critical.

If Robot B has fundamentally different kinematics (e.g., humanoid arm vs. gripper-on-a-rail), the action decoder cannot bridge the gap even with labeled examples, because no two-stage training can invent new joint types. The approach assumes the target embodiment can physically execute the same task as the source.

The paper trains on 1 million episodes across multiple embodiments simultaneously, so the video model sees many different robots solving the same task. At adaptation time, even a small set of Robot B labels (hundreds of trajectories) teaches the action decoder Robot B's personal translation. This works because embodiment-invariant task structure exists and is pervasive in real-world manipulation: the steps to grasp a cup are the same whether your arm is 1 meter or 1.2 meters long.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple simulation: a 2-joint robot arm on a table with a single target block. Train a video diffusion model on 5,000 recorded episodes of Robot A (arm length 1.0) successfully grasping the block from random starting poses. Then, without retraining the video model, train a lightweight action decoder on 200 episodes of Robot B (arm length 1.2, different gripper) doing the same task. Test both robots on held-out block positions and gripper angles. Measure success rate (block lifted) and action prediction error (predicted joint angle vs. true angle) on Robot B.
demo.closing: If the video model captures true embodiment-invariant task structure, Robot B with video pretraining should succeed on 80%+ of unseen poses, while Robot B trained from scratch succeeds on 20%. The gap is the transfer bonus.
